sections.title: The present: now, always, and soon

body.p: The Greek present covers more ground than the English present.

head: Use
Example
English
rows: What are you doing? I'm reading.
I live in Athens. I know.
I've been living here for two years.
I go in and what do I see?

ex.el: Μαθαίνω ελληνικά εδώ και έναν χρόνο.
ex.en: I've been learning Greek for a year.
How long have you been in Greece?
This afternoon we're going to the cinema.

body.tip: English "I have been doing X for..." is the **present** in Greek, with **εδώ και** or just a time phrase: **Δουλεύω εδώ και τρία χρόνια**, never *έχω δουλέψει τρία χρόνια* for a situation that is still going on.

check.q: "I've lived in Crete for five years (and still do)":
options: Έχω ζήσει στην Κρήτη πέντε χρόνια.
check.why: An ongoing situation uses the present: ζω (εδώ και) πέντε χρόνια.
The present can express a planned future.

sections.title: Simple past vs imperfect: the two pasts

body.p: Greek has two simple pasts, and the difference is **aspect**, not time.

head: Simple past (αόριστος): perfective
Imperfect (παρατατικός): imperfective
rows: "I was writing, I used to write"

ex.en: Yesterday I wrote a letter. (done, finished)
I was writing a letter when you came. (in progress)
Every summer we used to go to the village. (habit)

ex.el: Το καλοκαίρι του 2019 πήγαμε στο χωριό.
ex.en: In summer 2019 we went to the village. (one occasion)

body.p: **Story-telling** combines them: the imperfect sets the scene, the simple past gives the events.

ex.el: Έβρεχε και ο δρόμος ήταν άδειος. Ξαφνικά άκουσα ένα θόρυβο. Γύρισα και είδα έναν σκύλο.
ex.en: It was raining and the street was empty. Suddenly I heard a noise. I turned and saw a dog.

body.p: **Clues** that usually call for the simple past: χθες, πέρσι, ξαφνικά, μια φορά, μόλις, τελικά, τρεις φορές, για δύο ώρες (a bounded period). Clues for the imperfect: κάθε μέρα, συνήθως, πάντα, συχνά, όταν ήμουν μικρός, ενώ, την ώρα που.

body.tip: A stated duration does not force the imperfect. **Διάβασα δύο ώρες** presents the two hours as a finished block ("I read for two hours"); **Διάβαζα δύο ώρες** dwells on the activity while it lasted. Both are correct; the simple past is the usual choice when the period is over and the story moves on.

check.q: "When I was young I used to play football":
check.why: A habit in the past: imperfect έπαιζα.
A single sudden event: simple past έσβησε.

check.q: "While I was cooking, the phone rang":
check.why: Background (imperfect) + event (simple past).

body.p: **Θα** + verb forms the future. As with the past, there are two aspects:

head: Simple future (θα + dependent)
Continuous future (θα + present)
rows: Θα σου γράψω. I'll write to you.
Θα σου γράφω. I'll be writing to you (regularly).
Θα φάμε στις οχτώ. We'll eat at eight.
Θα τρώμε όταν έρθεις. We'll be eating when you come.
Αύριο θα διαβάσω το κεφάλαιο. I'll read the chapter tomorrow.
Αύριο όλη μέρα θα διαβάζω. Tomorrow I'll be studying all day.

ex.en: I'll be waiting for you. (ongoing)
I'll wait for you at five.
What will you do on Saturday?

ex.el: Από τον Σεπτέμβριο θα δουλεύω στην Αθήνα.
ex.en: From September I'll be working in Athens.

body.p: **Θα also expresses probability** (what is likely now or was likely in the past):

ex.en: It must be about nine.
(S)he must still be sleeping.
(S)he must have forgotten it.
(S)he will have left (probably).

body.p: **Θα is invariable**, never stressed, and goes before weak pronouns and after δεν: **Δεν θα σου το πω** "I won't tell you".

check.why: Repeated: continuous future θα τηλεφωνώ.
Θα + present can express a guess about now.

body.p: Modern Greek has no infinitive. Where English says "to do" after a verb (I want **to go**), Greek uses **να + subjunctive**, with the subject marked on the verb: **Θέλω να πάω** "I want to go", **Θέλω να πας** "I want you to go".

The subjunctive has the same two aspects: **να γράφω** (ongoing, general, repeated) and **να γράψω** (once, complete). **The simple (perfective) form is the default** when talking about a specific action.

ex.en: I want to learn Greek. (to achieve)
I like learning languages. (in general, ongoing)

ex.el: Μπορείς να μου πεις την ώρα;
ex.en: Can you tell me the time?
I have to leave.
You should eat more healthily. (in general)
I started reading. (ongoing activity)
(S)he stopped smoking.

body.p: **Verbs that naturally take the continuous** after να: verbs of beginning, continuing, stopping and habit: **αρχίζω, συνεχίζω, σταματάω, κόβω (quit), συνηθίζω, μαθαίνω (learn how to)**: **Έμαθα να κολυμπάω** "I learned to swim".

**Verbs and phrases followed by να:** θέλω, μπορώ, πρέπει, πρόκειται, ξέρω (how to), προσπαθώ, σκοπεύω, ελπίζω, φοβάμαι, ζητάω, λέω (tell to), αποφασίζω, ξεχνάω, θυμάμαι, αρνούμαι, μου αρέσει, είναι δύσκολο / εύκολο / σημαντικό.

check.why: The person goes on the verb after να: να έρθεις.
Learning a skill takes the continuous: να κολυμπάω.

body.p: **Positive commands** use the imperative, in two aspects:

list: **Simple (perfective)**: one action now. **Κλείσε την πόρτα!** "Close the door!" **Πες μου!** "Tell me!"
**Continuous**: an ongoing or repeated instruction, or a general rule. **Κλείνε την πόρτα όταν βγαίνεις!** "Close the door (every time) you go out!" **Διάβαζε κάθε μέρα** "Study every day".

body.p: **Negative commands** use **μη(ν) + subjunctive** (no να):

ex.en: Don't worry. (in general)
Don't forget the keys! (this time)
Don't talk so loudly.
Don't touch it!

body.p: **Other persons and softened commands** use **να** (or **ας** for "let"):

ex.en: Take care! / Be careful! (to someone leaving)
Do write to me.
Let's go!
Let him wait.
Let's not discuss it.

body.p: **Polite requests** are softened with **μπορείτε να...;**, **θα μπορούσατε να...;**, **θα ήθελα...**, **παρακαλώ**: **Θα μπορούσατε να μου φέρετε τον λογαριασμό;** "Could you bring me the bill?"

check.why: Negative command: μην + subjunctive.
"Let's" is ας + 1st plural (να φάμε is possible as a suggestion too, but ας φάμε is the standard "let's").

sections.title: The perfect tenses: when Greek uses them

body.p: The Greek **present perfect** (έχω γράψει) is used less than the English one. Greek often uses the **simple past** where English uses "have done", especially with a recent event.

head: English
Natural Greek
rows: Have you ever been to Crete?

body.p: **Use the present perfect** for experience up to now (**ποτέ, ακόμα, ήδη, ως τώρα, πολλές φορές**), and for a past action whose result matters now, especially in formal speech:

ex.en: Have you read Kazantzakis?
I haven't finished yet.

ex.el: Έχω πάει τρεις φορές στη Σαντορίνη.
ex.en: I've been to Santorini three times.
The government has taken measures.

body.p: **Never** use the present perfect with a specific past time: *Έχω έρθει χθες* is wrong; say **Ήρθα χθες**.
**The pluperfect** (είχα γράψει) places one past action before another, as in English:

ex.el: Όταν φτάσαμε, η ταινία είχε αρχίσει.
ex.en: When we arrived, the film had started.

ex.el: Δεν είχα ξαναδεί τόσο ωραίο ηλιοβασίλεμα.
ex.en: I had never seen such a beautiful sunset.

body.p: **The future perfect** (θα έχω γράψει) is an action completed before a future point, or a guess about the past:

ex.el: Μέχρι το βράδυ θα έχω τελειώσει.
ex.en: By evening I will have finished.
(S)he must have arrived by now.

check.why: A definite past time: simple past.
Experience up to now (ποτέ): present perfect.

body.p: Greek conditionals use **αν** (or **εάν**, formal) "if", and their meaning depends on the tense and aspect in both parts.
**1. Real or likely (future or general):** αν + subjunctive-type form, main clause in the future, present or imperative.

ex.en: If it rains, we'll stay home.

ex.el: Αν έχεις χρόνο, πέρασε από το γραφείο.
ex.en: If you have time, drop by the office.
If you heat ice, it melts.

body.p: Note: **αν βρέξει** uses the perfective dependent form without να, exactly like θα βρέξει.
**2. Unlikely or imaginary (present / future):** αν + imperfect, main clause **θα + imperfect** (the conditional).

ex.el: Αν είχα λεφτά, θα αγόραζα σπίτι στο νησί.
ex.en: If I had money, I would buy a house on the island.

ex.el: Αν ήμουν στη θέση σου, θα του μιλούσα.
ex.en: If I were you, I would talk to him.

body.p: **3. Unreal past (counterfactual):** αν + pluperfect (or imperfect), main clause **θα + pluperfect** (or imperfect).

ex.el: Αν είχες έρθει, θα είχες περάσει ωραία.
ex.en: If you had come, you would have had a good time.

ex.el: Αν το ήξερα, θα σου το έλεγα.
ex.en: If I had known, I would have told you. (also: if I knew, I would tell you)

body.p: The imperfect in both clauses (type 2 forms) can refer to either the present or the past; context decides. The pluperfect forms make the past meaning unambiguous.

**Other conditional words:** **αν και** "although" (not a conditional!), **εκτός αν** "unless", **σε περίπτωση που** "in case", **με την προϋπόθεση ότι / να** "provided that", **αρκεί να** "as long as", **ακόμα κι αν** "even if".

ex.en: I'll come, unless it rains.

ex.el: Μπορείς να βγεις, αρκεί να γυρίσεις νωρίς.
ex.en: You can go out, as long as you come back early.

check.q: "If I won the lottery, I'd travel":
options: Αν κερδίσω το λαχείο, θα ταξιδέψω.
Αν κέρδιζα το λαχείο, θα ταξίδευα.
check.answer: Αν κέρδιζα το λαχείο, θα ταξίδευα.
check.why: An imaginary condition: αν + imperfect, θα + imperfect.

check.q: "If you had told me, I would have helped":
options: Αν μου είχες πει, θα σε είχα βοηθήσει.
check.answer: Αν μου είχες πει, θα σε είχα βοηθήσει.
check.why: Unreal past: pluperfect in both clauses.

body.p: **Wishes** use **να** or **μακάρι να**:

ex.en: Be well! (thanks, wishing health)
Long life to you! (on a name day or birthday)
I hope (s)he comes.
I wish you were here. (unreal present: imperfect)

ex.el: Μακάρι να το είχα μάθει νωρίτερα.
ex.en: If only I had found out sooner. (unreal past: pluperfect)

body.p: **Regrets and reproaches** use **θα / έπρεπε να / μπορούσες να** + past forms:

ex.en: I should have told you.
You should have come.
You could have let me know.
I'd better not have said it.

body.p: **The polite conditional** softens requests and opinions: **θα ήθελα** "I would like", **θα μπορούσα** "I could", **θα έλεγα** "I would say", **θα πρότεινα** "I'd suggest".

ex.en: I'd like a glass of water.
I'd say you're right.

check.why: An unreal present wish: μακάρι να + imperfect (είχα).

options: Έπρεπε να με πάρεις. / Έπρεπε να με είχες πάρει.
check.why: Έπρεπε να + dependent or pluperfect both express a past obligation not fulfilled.

sections.title: Time clauses: όταν, μόλις, πριν, αφού, ενώ

body.p: Time clauses about the **future** use the dependent form (no θα), like English "when I arrive", not "when I will arrive":

ex.en: When I arrive, I'll phone you.
As soon as you finish, come.
Before you leave, close the windows.
After we eat, we'll go out.

ex.el: Μέχρι να γυρίσει, θα έχω τελειώσει.
ex.en: By the time (s)he returns, I'll have finished.

body.p: **Πριν** takes **να** before a verb (**πριν να φύγεις** is also heard, **πριν φύγεις** is standard); **μέχρι / ώσπου / ωσότου** take **να** for "until": **Περίμενε μέχρι να έρθω** "Wait until I come".

**Aspect in time clauses:** **όταν + simple** = "once, at the moment that" (**Όταν τον είδα, χάρηκα** "When I saw him, I was glad"); **όταν + continuous** = "whenever, during" (**Όταν τον έβλεπα, χαιρόμουν** "Whenever I saw him, I was glad").
**Ενώ** "while, whereas" takes the indicative: **Ενώ διάβαζα, αποκοιμήθηκα** "While I was reading, I fell asleep". **Καθώς** "as" is similar and slightly more literary.

check.q: "When you get to Athens, call me":
options: Όταν θα φτάσεις στην Αθήνα, πάρε με.
Όταν φτάσεις στην Αθήνα, πάρε με.
check.answer: Όταν φτάσεις στην Αθήνα, πάρε με.
check.why: Future time clauses drop θα: όταν φτάσεις.
Μέχρι + να + dependent form.

body.p: Greek reports statements with **ότι / πως** + the **same tense** the speaker used. There is no automatic "back-shift" as in English.

head: Direct
Reported
rows: Είπε ότι είναι κουρασμένος. (He said he was tired.)
Είπε ότι θα έρθει. (She said she would come.)
Μου είπε ότι το είδε. (He told me he had seen it.)

body.p: When the original future is reported from a past viewpoint, **θα + imperfect** (the conditional) is also used, as in English "would": **Είπε ότι θα ερχόταν** "She said she would come (but...)", often implying the plan did not happen.
**Reported questions** use **αν** "whether" or the question word: **Με ρώτησε αν θέλω καφέ** "He asked me if I wanted coffee". **Δεν ξέρω πού μένει** "I don't know where (s)he lives".
**Reported commands** use **να**: **Μου είπε να περιμένω** "(S)he told me to wait". **Τους ζήτησα να μην αργήσουν** "I asked them not to be late".

**Reporting verbs with nuance**: **ισχυρίζομαι ότι** claim, **υποστηρίζω ότι** maintain, **παραδέχομαι ότι** admit, **αρνούμαι ότι** deny, **διευκρινίζω ότι** clarify, **υπογραμμίζω ότι** stress, **επισημαίνω ότι** point out, **δηλώνω ότι** declare, **φέρεται να** "is reported to" (journalistic).

ex.el: Ο υπουργός φέρεται να έχει παραιτηθεί.
ex.en: The minister is reported to have resigned.
(S)he denied knowing the suspect.

check.why: Greek can keep the original tense (είναι) or shift it; keeping it is common in speech.
A reported command uses να.

sections.title: Aspect in depth: choosing continuous or simple

body.p: The aspect choice outside the indicative past is where advanced learners still slip. Some guiding principles:
**1. Simple (perfective) is the default** for a specific, single action after θα, να, μη, ας, όταν, αν: **θα πάω, να δεις, μην πέσεις, ας φύγουμε, όταν τελειώσεις**.
**2. Continuous (imperfective) when the action is**:

list: repeated or habitual: **Θα σου γράφω κάθε μέρα.**
ongoing for a stretch of time: **Θα δουλεύω όλο το βράδυ.**
a general rule or advice: **Να τρως φρούτα. Μην πίνεις πολύ.**
an activity rather than a result: **Αρχίζω να διαβάζω.**

body.p: **3. Verbs of state** (ξέρω, είμαι, έχω, θέλω, μένω, πιστεύω) have no meaningful perfective in most uses, or change meaning: **ξέρω** know vs **μαθαίνω/έμαθα** come to know; **θέλω** want vs **θέλησα** decided to; **μπορούσα** I was able (ability) vs **μπόρεσα** I managed (on one occasion); **ήξερα** I knew vs **έμαθα** I found out.

ex.en: I could (used to be able to) swim kilometres.
I managed to persuade him.
I knew it. / I found out yesterday.

body.p: **4. Negative commands**: **μη γράφεις** "stop writing / don't (ever) write"; **μη γράψεις** "don't write (this time)".

check.why: Success on one occasion: simple past μπόρεσα.
A general habit: continuous να πίνεις. (Να πιεις would mean on one occasion, now.)

sections.title: Mood in subordinate clauses: ότι vs να, που vs να

body.p: Some contrasts in subordinate clauses depend on mood:
**ότι / πως (fact) vs να (possibility, wish, purpose):**

ex.en: I know that (s)he swims. (fact)
I know how to swim. (ability)
(S)he says (s)he's coming.
(S)he says we should come.

body.p: **Relative clause with να: an unknown or hypothetical antecedent.**

ex.el: Ψάχνω ένα σπίτι που έχει κήπο.
ex.en: I'm looking for a (specific) house that has a garden.

ex.el: Ψάχνω ένα σπίτι που να έχει κήπο.
ex.en: I'm looking for a house with a garden (any, if one exists).

ex.el: Δεν υπάρχει κανείς που να μην το ξέρει.
ex.en: There's no one who doesn't know it.

body.p: **Purpose and result:** **για να** "in order to", **ώστε να** "so that, so as to", **τόσο ... που** "so ... that" (result, indicative).

ex.en: I came to see you.

ex.el: Μίλα πιο αργά, ώστε να σε καταλάβουν.
ex.en: Speak more slowly so that they understand you.

ex.el: Ήταν τόσο κουρασμένος που κοιμήθηκε αμέσως.
ex.en: He was so tired that he fell asleep immediately.

body.p: **Emotion and fear:** **Φοβάμαι ότι** "I fear that (it's so)"; **φοβάμαι μήπως / μη(ν)** "I'm afraid that (it might)": **Φοβάμαι μήπως αργήσουμε** "I'm afraid we might be late". **Χαίρομαι που ήρθες** "I'm glad (that) you came" uses **που** after emotions.

check.q: "I'm looking for someone who speaks Greek (anyone)":
options: Ψάχνω κάποιον που να μιλάει ελληνικά.
check.answer: Ψάχνω κάποιον που να μιλάει ελληνικά.
check.why: A hypothetical person: που + να.
After emotions, που is the natural choice. (Ότι is possible but less idiomatic.)

body.p: **Θα + imperfect** (the conditional) does much more than "would":

head: Use
Example
Meaning
rows: I'd have come if you'd invited me.
Θα ήταν δέκα η ώρα όταν έφυγε.
It must have been ten when (s)he left.
Κάθε βράδυ θα καθόταν στο μπαλκόνι.
Every evening he would sit on the balcony.

body.p: **Counterfactuals without αν.** Greek can express an unreal condition with a participle or a phrase: **Χωρίς τη βοήθειά σου, θα είχα αποτύχει** "Without your help, I would have failed"; **Στη θέση σου, δεν θα το έκανα** "In your place, I wouldn't do it"; **Να το ήξερα, θα ερχόμουν** "Had I known, I would have come" (να + imperfect = "if only / if").

ex.el: Να ήξερα ότι θα βρέξει, θα έπαιρνα ομπρέλα.
ex.en: Had I known it would rain, I'd have taken an umbrella.

body.p: **Concessive conditionals:** **ακόμα κι αν / και να** "even if": **Και να μου το ζητήσεις, δεν θα το κάνω** "Even if you ask me, I won't do it". **Ό,τι κι αν γίνει** "whatever happens". **Όσο κι αν προσπαθήσω** "however hard I try".

**Aspect for style.** Writers exploit aspect for effect: the **imperfect** for slow description and "camera" narration, the **historic present** for drama, the **simple past** for pace. In formal reports, the **present perfect** presents results as relevant now (**έχει σημειωθεί αύξηση** "an increase has been recorded").

check.q: Να το ήξερα, θα σου το έλεγα means:
options: Had I known, I would have told you.
I will tell you when I know.
check.answer: Had I known, I would have told you.
check.why: Να + imperfect can introduce an unreal condition.

options: Όσο κι αν προσπαθήσω, δεν μπορώ.
check.answer: Όσο κι αν προσπαθήσω, δεν μπορώ.
check.why: Concessive: όσο κι αν + dependent form.

sections.title: Tense, aspect and register in formal Greek

body.p: Formal and journalistic Greek has characteristic verbal habits:

list: **The present perfect for news**: **Έχουν καταγραφεί δεκάδες περιστατικά** "Dozens of cases have been recorded".

**Passive impersonals with να or ότι**: **Αναμένεται να ανακοινωθεί** "It is expected to be announced"; **Φέρεται ότι / να** "is reported"; **Εκτιμάται ότι** "It is estimated that"; **Λέγεται ότι** "It is said that".
**Πρόκειται να** "is going to, is due to" for scheduled future: **Η συνάντηση πρόκειται να γίνει την Τρίτη**.
**Επρόκειτο να** "was going to, was due to": **Επρόκειτο να υπογραφεί η συμφωνία, όταν...**
**Έμελλε να** "was destined to" (literary): **Έμελλε να γίνει ο μεγαλύτερος ποιητής της γενιάς του** "He was destined to become the greatest poet of his generation".
**The future of intention in plans and laws**: **Η ρύθμιση θα ισχύσει από 1η Ιανουαρίου** "The arrangement will apply from 1 January".

ex.el: Αναμένεται να ψηφιστεί μέσα στον μήνα.
ex.en: It is expected to be voted on within the month.

ex.el: Οι συνομιλίες πρόκειται να συνεχιστούν αύριο.
ex.en: The talks are due to continue tomorrow.

body.p: **Ας** in formal argument: **Ας εξετάσουμε...** "Let us examine...", **Ας σημειωθεί ότι...** "Let it be noted that...", **Ας μην ξεχνάμε ότι...** "Let us not forget that...".

check.q: "The law is expected to be passed":
check.why: Passive impersonal: αναμένεται να + dependent passive.

check.q: "The meeting is due to take place on Monday":
options: Η συνάντηση είναι να γίνει τη Δευτέρα.
Η συνάντηση πρόκειται να γίνει τη Δευτέρα.
check.answer: Η συνάντηση πρόκειται να γίνει τη Δευτέρα.
check.why: Scheduled future: πρόκειται να.

el: Το ρήμα Β΄: χρόνοι, όψη, εγκλίσεις
title: The verb II: tense, aspect and mood
blurb: What each tense means, the logic of aspect, θα and να, conditionals, wishes, commands and reported speech.

intro.p: The first verb document showed how to build the forms. This one explains **what they mean**. Greek verbs answer three questions at once:

list: **Tense (χρόνος):** is the action past or non-past?
**Aspect (όψη):** is the action seen as ongoing or repeated (**imperfective / continuous**), or as a single complete whole (**perfective / simple**)?
**Mood (έγκλιση):** is it a fact (indicative), a possibility, wish or purpose (subjunctive with να), or a command (imperative)?

intro.p: English expresses aspect only partly ("I was writing" vs "I wrote"). Greek marks it in **every** form outside the present: the past, the future, the subjunctive and the imperative all come in a continuous and a simple version. Choosing between them is the single most important skill for sounding natural, so this document returns to it again and again.
